claim:
For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(X_n\) be the real normed plane whose unit ball is the regular Euclidean \(2n\)-gon with vertices
\[
v_j=\bigl(\cos(j\pi/n),\sin(j\pi/n)\bigr),\qquad 0\le j<2n.
\]
Write \(\beta_n=\pi/(2n)\), and put \(q_j=1\) if \(j\) is even and \(q_j=\sec\beta_n\) if \(j\) is odd. For every real \(t\ge0\), its classical modulus of smoothness is exactly
\[
\rho_{X_n}(t)=\max_{0\le j\le n}
\left[q_j\cos(j\beta_n)+tq_{n-j}\sin(j\beta_n)\right]-1.
\]
Moreover, the same two unit vertices
\[
x=v_0,\qquad y=v_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
\]
attain the defining supremum for every \(t\ge0\); the maximizing pair need not change when the active affine branch changes. In particular, for the regular decagonal plane \(X_5\), let
\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\quad
s=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\quad
a=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4},\quad
b=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}.
\]
Then its complete scale profile is the sharp four-phase law
\[
\rho_{X_5}(t)=
\begin{cases}
s t,&0\le t\le\varphi^{-1},\\
a+b t-1,&\varphi^{-1}\le t\le1,\\
b+a t-1,&1\le t\le\varphi,\\
t+s-1,&t\ge\varphi.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular \(\rho_{X_5}(1)=(3\sqrt5-5)/4\), and the fixed pair \((v_0,v_2)\) attains the entire decagonal profile. This statement asserts existence of a universal maximizing vertex pair, not uniqueness or a complete classification of all maximizers.

correctness.rationale: For \(B_n=\operatorname{conv}\{v_j\}\), its polar is the regular polygon with vertices \(w_j=\sec\beta R_\beta v_j\). Taking independent norming functionals for the two terms in the definition and maximizing over both primal balls gives exactly \(1+\rho(t)=\frac12\max_{f,g\in B_n^*}(N_n^*(f+g)+tN_n^*(f-g))\). Separate convexity attains the maximum at polar vertices; the scalar-rotation identification of the polar with the primal then gives the two chord norms. Their directions have parity-dependent vertex/side-midpoint gauges, yielding the stated max of n+1 affine functions. The maximizing primal support directions for a polar vertex pair are orthogonal. The nearest vertices to such orthogonal rays can always be selected with mesh-step difference \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), proving that the same canonical vertex pair attains every scale. In the decagon the dominated end branches and the three consecutive exact crossings produce the stated four-phase law without inference from sampled data.
risks: The existence argument for a fixed maximizer does not classify all equality pairs.
No conclusion for arbitrary nonregular polygonal norms or for dimension greater than two.

originality.rationale: The same regular 2n-gons appear in complete 2023 primary work, but that work determines norming-functional diameter and therefore only the infinitesimal slope information of the classical modulus; its main statements do not yield an all-scale envelope or a permanent maximizer without a new independent dual maximization. Complete 2010 and 2015 primary papers treat general smoothness functions and supporting-modulus asymptotics, not exact polygon profiles. A 2024 survey treats the classical definition and a distinct midpoint-deficit modulus but has no regular-polygon computation. Targeted indexed and general searches for the entire regular decagon profile, golden-ratio breakpoints, dual formulations and aliases returned no stronger equivalent statement. This is evidence for noncoverage, not proof of universal novelty.

value.rationale: The classical Day modulus is a standard quantitative invariant governing uniform smoothness and its dual convexity relations. Regular even polygons form the canonical finite-dimensional approximation of the Euclidean circle, and the new formula supplies every scale for every polygon, not just a finite table or a single parameter slice. The additional existence of the same near-orthogonal vertex pair for all scales is a strong structural simplification of the global two-vector optimization. For the regular decagon the function has four distinct sharp affine regimes separated by golden-ratio parameters, demonstrating meaningful finite-scale behavior absent from the known first-order norming-functional diameter.
risks: The general finite-envelope theorem does not give a compact four-phase form for every n; only the decagon case is fully expanded.
This is a sharp geometric profile, not a new downstream fixed-point theorem or a general renorming result.
